extracted.intended_audience: poets, critics, and educated readers interested in heroic/epic poetry (especially writers of blank verse)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the diction, syntax, and metrical practices appropriate to a heroic/epic poem (with special attention to blank verse), using Milton's Paradise Lost as the primary example. Advises how to balance clarity and elevation, specific stylistic devices, and moderation in unusual usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of an Heroic Poem: Perspicuous and Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: It is requisite that the Language of an Heroic Poem should be both Perspicuous and Sublime. In proportion as either of these two Qualities are wanting, the Language is imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perspicuity and sublimity are the two primary, co‑required qualities; deficiency in either renders the language imperfect. Throughout the essay this serves as the organizing principle for all further prescriptions and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity (clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspicuity is the first and most necessary Qualification; insomuch that a good-natur'd Reader sometimes overlooks a little Slip even in the Grammar or Syntax, where it is impossible for him to mistake the Poet's Sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clear expression of thought; small grammatical slips may be forgiven when the sense is large and natural. Examples given where syntax could confuse but is excused because thought is great. Do not sacrifice intelligibility for ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ordinary idiomatic phrases (guard against idiomatick ways of speaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Poet should take particular Care to guard himself against Idiomatick Ways of Speaking; the most obvious and conversational phrases may become too familiar and contract a kind of Meanness by passing through the Mouths of the Vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid common conversational idioms and first phrases that present themselves; such usages can debase poetry. Examples cited: Ovid and Lucan's ‘poornesses of expression’ from taking the first phrase that offered. Use elevated alternatives when plain speech would sound too familiar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity must deviate from common forms but avoid false affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Language of an Epic should be Sublime: it ought to deviate from common Forms and ordinary Phrases of Speech, yet the Poet must not swell into a false Sublime by endeavouring to avoid the other extreme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depart from common speech to achieve sublimity, but avoid stiff, unnatural, or affected grandeur. Cautions: Æschylus (sometimes), Sophocles, Claudian, Statius, Shakespeare, Lee cited as examples where affectation harms perspicuity. Seek a balance between elevation and naturalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphors to raise language
rubrics_metrics.description: First, by the Use of Metaphors: such are those of Milton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ bold but just metaphors to elevate diction. Metaphors should not be so thickly sown as to clash with one another (which would turn a sentence into an enigma or riddle). Prefer metaphors that are apt and do not obscure sense; Milton’s metaphors are praised for boldness and correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use idioms and forms from other tongues (Hellenisms, Latinisms, Hebraisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another way of raising the Language is to make use of the Idioms of other Tongues. Milton has infused a great many Latinisms, as well as Græcisms, and sometimes Hebraisms, into the Language of his Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating foreign idioms and constructions can give a poetical turn and elevate diction (e.g., Latinisms, Greek forms). Use such forms to depart from vulgar speech and produce greater sound and solemnity; follow ancient practice (Virgil, Homer). Moderation and appropriateness to the language's genius are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition and syntactic variation (adjective placement, adjective→substantive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under this head may be reckon'd the placing the Adjective after the Substantive, the Transposition of Words, the turning the Adjective into a Substantive, with several other Foreign Modes of Speech...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syntactic inversions and nominalizations to produce a more elevated, poetic sound and to distinguish verse from prose. These foreign modes of speech should be naturalized carefully to enhance tone without confusing readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lengthening/shortening phrases and manipulating syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: The lengthning of a Phrase by the Addition of Words... as also by the extending or contracting of particular Words by the Insertion or Omission of certain Syllables. Milton has put in practice this Method...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary phrase length by adding or omitting words or syllables to create variety and musicality. Employ elisions and contractions judiciously (e.g., occasional suppression of a syllable, discussed elision of initial y) to vary numbers and avoid monotony; do not overapply to the point of inaccuracy or obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of the noblest words and use of archaic vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton, by the above-mentioned Helps, and by the Choice of the noblest Words and Phrases which our Tongue would afford him, has carried our Language to a greater Height... The same Reason recommended to him several old Words, which also makes his Poem appear the more venerable, and gives it a greater Air of Antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select elevated, noble vocabulary and consider archaic or venerable words to confer dignity and an air of antiquity. Such choice should support sublimity and the epic tone, but be balanced with perspicuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coining neologisms sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: I must likewise take notice, that there are in Milton several Words of his own coining, as Cerberean, miscreated, Hell-doom'd, Embryon Atoms, and many others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neologisms can be effective when used by a great poet and have classical precedent (Homer). They should be used with restraint and judged for aptness; readers displeased by invention may be reminded that ancient poets did the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pomp of sound and energy of expression necessary for blank verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Verse is not built upon Rhymes, there Pomp of Sound, and Energy of Expression, are indispensably necessary to support the Stile, and keep it from falling into the Flatness of Prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blank verse requires sonic grandeur and energetic diction (pomp, energy) to distinguish it from prose and sustain long narrative lines. Rhyme can mask ordinary phrasing; without rhyme, stronger devices of sound and diction are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety in numbers (meter) to avoid monotony
rubrics_metrics.description: He has varied his Numbers in such a manner, as makes them incapable of satiating the Ear, and cloying the Reader, which the same uniform Measure would certainly have done...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce metrical variety—elisions, alterations in syllabic count, rhythmic variation—to prevent monotony in long narrative verse. Innovations in measure should enliven the ear but be used with sensitivity to natural speech and sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and judicious intermixture of unusual words and devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A judicious intermixture is requisite ... In the employment of all the species of unusual words, moderation is necessary: for metaphors, foreign words, or any of the others improperly used, and with a design to be ridiculous, would produce the same effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is essential: a temperate mix of metaphors, foreign words, archaic forms, and syntactic variations produces sublimity without turning language into enigma or barbarous jargon. Avoid extremes—either plainness that becomes mean, or excess that becomes unintelligible.
